title: UPI Merchant Charges Deferred Until After Diwali: The 0.4% Fee That Was Due October 15 Is on Hold
excerpt: NPCI's steering committee pushed the merchant discount rate on select UPI payments past the festive season, with a new date to be notified. What was planned: 0.4% on merchant transactions above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300, with person-to-person transfers and small payments exempt — and merchants barred from passing the fee to customers.
body:
• NPCI announced on Tuesday that merchant discount rate (MDR) charges on select person-to-merchant UPI transactions will not begin on October 15 as scheduled, and will instead be implemented immediately after Diwali on a date to be notified separately.
  • The proposed charge is 0.4% on eligible merchant transactions above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 and above; person-to-person transfers and merchant payments up to ₹2,000 remain exempt.
  • The fee is paid by merchants, and the framework bars them from passing it to customers — a shopper paying by UPI should see no extra charge at the till.
  • The deferral, decided by the UPI and Services Steering Committee citing the festive season, follows pushback from trade bodies and payments firms; RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said on October 7 that a small MDR was unlikely to dent UPI volumes.

The return of merchant charges on UPI has been postponed past India's biggest shopping season. The National Payments Corporation of India said on Tuesday that its UPI and Services Steering Committee had decided, "keeping in mind the festive season," that the merchant discount rate on select person-to-merchant UPI transactions "shall be implemented immediately post Diwali at a date to be notified separately." The charge had been due to start on October 15 — two days after the announcement — and NPCI managing director and CEO Dilip Asbe confirmed the deferral to Mint.

What was about to change

On September 15, the government announced the reintroduction of MDR on select UPI transactions, reversing the zero-MDR policy in place since January 2020. Under the proposed framework, eligible merchant transactions above ₹2,000 would attract a fee of 0.4%, with a maximum charge of ₹300 on transactions of ₹75,000 and above, and a flat ₹5 proposed for select categories. Person-to-person transfers were to stay free, merchant payments up to ₹2,000 exempt, and small merchants with monthly UPI turnover up to ₹1 lakh excluded. MDR is the processing fee merchants pay banks and payment providers; the deferred question is whether India's free-UPI model can be made sustainable for the companies that run it without taxing the transaction itself.

https://x.com/ETNOWlive/status/2109971678520344869

Why it was deferred

The timing was the problem. Diwali is the peak of India's retail calendar, and merchant bodies, fintech companies and payments firms pressed for a delay, arguing that new charges risked dampening consumer sentiment and complicating the highest-volume weeks of the year — and that banks, payment service providers and merchants needed more preparation time. The official counter-argument has not changed: on October 7, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said a small MDR fee was unlikely to have a major effect on UPI volumes, noting no decline at that point. NPCI has not said whether rates or thresholds will change with the new date, and businesses have been advised to wait for the formal implementation circular before deciding which of their transactions will attract the charge. For shoppers, the bottom line for this Diwali is simple: UPI stays exactly as free as it was.
